title: 12-year-old foreign tourist missing in Japan, police asking for help finding her [Video]
description: U.K. middle schooler seen on security camera footage after leaving family’s rental property alone. Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, a 12-year-old middle school student from the U.K., arrived in Japan for sightseeing with her parents and older brother on July 21. content:
U.K. middle schooler seen on security camera footage after leaving family’s rental property alone.

Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, a 12-year-old middle school student from the U.K., arrived in Japan for sightseeing with her parents and older brother on July 21. She has now been reported missing, and the police are asking for help in finding her.

The Paul family is currently staying at a private rental property in Tokyo’s Kamata neighborhood. The last time the family saw Carmelita was on the night of August 12, when her father spoke with her before going to bed. When the rest of the family woke up at around 8:30 on August 13, she was gone.

▼ Video showing a photo of Carmelita released by the police as part of the call for help locating her

Carmelita did not take a phone with her when she left, so the family had no way of contacting her. The family contacted the police shortly before 9:30. In examining surveillance camera recordings the police found images of Carmelita, dressed in a sky-blue sleeveless top, black-and-white checked skirt and black pumps, and carrying a pink handbag, walking in the Nichome section of Kamata, near the family’s rental property. Investigators were able to determine that she passed through Yokohama Station, roughly 20 minutes south by train from Kamata Station, later that same morning, but have been unable to trace her path any farther than that.

Carmelita did not take her passport with her when she left the rental property, and her family estimates she had only a few thousand yen (less than US$100) on her, which would not be enough for an extended stay in reputable lodgings. The Tokyo/Yokohama area has also been experiencing severe rain showers , making proper shelter even more important than it would usually be.

The police describe Carmelita as being roughly 160 centimeters (5 feet, 3 inches) in height, with a medium build and curly black hair. Anyone with information as to her whereabouts is asked to contact the Tokyo Metropolitan Police’s Kamata Station at the phone number 03-3731-0110, but information can also be submitted at any police box or station.

title: Pokémon donuts are coming to Krispy Kreme in the U.S. [Photos]
description: Pikachu, the original starter trio, and one more old-school Pokémon are getting ready to warm fans’ hearts and satisfy your sweet cravings. We recently found out that McDonald’s is going to be offering Happy Meals with crossover Hello Kitty/Godzilla figures later this month at its branches in the U.S., and while we’re obviously happy that […]
content:
Pikachu, the original starter trio, and one more old-school Pokémon are getting ready to warm fans’ hearts and satisfy your sweet cravings.

We recently found out that McDonald’s is going to be offering Happy Meals with crossover Hello Kitty/Godzilla figures later this month at its branches in the U.S., and while we’re obviously happy that people will have their burger and adorable toy needs covered, there is still one critical culinary component missing: dessert. Thankfully, after having your appetite whetted for adorable Japanese pop culture tie-ins, you can continue right on to Krispy Kreme, which has revealed that it’ll soon start selling Pokémon donuts in the U.S.

Offered as part of the ongoing 30th anniversary celebration of the Pokémon franchise, Krispy Kreme will be baking up a half-dozen different themed treats, starting with, naturally, a Pikachu donut featuring vanilla icing and a lemon cream filling.

All three of the Gen 1 starters are here too, Bulbasaur’s donut is the simplest, essentially one of Krispy Kreme’s flagship Original Glazed donuts enhanced with colorful vanilla icing and “leaves” made of frosting.

The Charmander donut gets caramel icing and a toasted marshmallow filling as a nod to the Fire-type’s powers.

Squirtle’s is the most elaborate-looking of the three starters’ donuts, with a swirl of cotton candy-flavor buttercream and sanding sugar.

The above-listed quartet often serve as ambassadors for the Pokémon franchise as a whole, and when there’s room for one more in a collection, the nod often goes to Eevee or whichever Pocket Monster species is having a moment, like Snorlax or Ditto are right now with their prominent roles in Pokémon Sleep and Pokémon Pokopia. However, Krispy Kreme has instead recruited Jigglypuff, who serves as the inspiration for a strawberry buttercream-topped donut with strawberry cookie crumbles.

Finally, rounding out the lineup of a half-dozen Pokémon donuts is an Original Glazed cosplaying as a Poké Ball thanks to vanilla and chocolate icing plus a whole bunch of crimson sprinkles.

Each of the species-specific Pokémon donuts also comes with a little paper decoration of its associated Pokémon. They’ll also be gracing the cups of Krispy Kreme’s donut holes…

…and Pokémon-theming will be showing up on Krispy Kreme boxes as well.

Krispy Kreme’s Pokémon donuts go on sale in the U.S. on August 18, the exact same day as McDonald’s Sanrio/kaiju Happy Meals.

title: 7-Eleven Japan has a “Super Spicy! Taiwan Mince Cutlet” that’s fiery red… but how hot is it?
description: Spoiler alert: Your taste buds aren’t ready for this convenience store katsu. One of the great things about convenience stores is their wide variety of hot food, giving us a simple way to pick up a snack that’s easy to eat while on the go. Not all the hot food is that easy to eat, […]
content:
Spoiler alert: Your taste buds aren’t ready for this convenience store katsu.

One of the great things about convenience stores is their wide variety of hot food, giving us a simple way to pick up a snack that’s easy to eat while on the go. Not all the hot food is that easy to eat, though, as we recently found out when we stumbled upon 7-Eleven’s “Super Spicy! Taiwan Mince Cutlet”, which practically burnt the taste buds off our tongue with a level of spiciness we weren’t expecting.

Things started off easy, as we spotted the fried cutlet in the hot food display and were instantly drawn to its fiery red appearance. As ardent spice lovers who’ve rarely been challenged by self-proclaimed “super spicy” products before, we casually picked one up to find out how mild it would be, but when we took a bite we immediately swallowed our pride.

From that very first bite, it felt like a flame had been ignited on the tip of our tongue, and the fire quickly spread to cover the entire palate, burning with an intensity that never let up. Surprisingly, it wasn’t just the fried coating that delivered the spicy hit, as the heat came from inside the minced-meat filling as well, giving us double the burn, for twice as long.

▼ Amidst the pain, our taste buds battled against the heat to assess the flavour, because for us, that’s the true marker for a really good hot product.

As it turns out, the flavour was one of the highlights – the filling contained a generous amount of juicy meat, with garlic chives adding an extra element of taste to make the whole thing even more delicious. Perhaps because of the minced meat and garlic chives, the cutlet had a vaguely gyoza-like flavour. Either way, both the taste and the heat were excellent, especially when combined with the wonderfully crispy coating, which crunched satisfyingly between the teeth with every bite.

▼ However, there was one thing that eluded us: what exactly makes it “Taiwan”?

We weren’t sure what the “Taiwan” in “Taiwan Mince Cutlet” was referring to, but after checking 7-Eleven Japan’s official site, we learned that the filling is “Taiwan Minchi” (“Taiwan Mince”) a spicy seasoned minced meat originating in Nagoya. So, in the end, the “Taiwan” in the name refers to the spicy and savoury minced meat filling used in dishes like Taiwan ramen from Nagoya’s famous Misen restaurant.

That’s also why it’s called a “minchi cutlet” rather than “menchi katsu”, which is the usual term for a Japanese-style minced-meat cutlet. It’s also the reason why the filling contains garlic chives, which you don’t normally find in a Japanese-style menchi katsu.

What started out as a chance encounter turned into an exciting journey of discovery, as we not only found out that the cutlet was hotter than any other convenience-store hot food we can remember trying, but also that its name pays homage to the “Taiwan” mince associated with Nagoya’s famed local food culture.

Priced at 189 yen (US$1.18), the Super Spicy! Taiwan Mince Cutlet really does live up to its name, so be sure to stop by your local 7-Eleven soon if you’re game enough to try it, as it’s only available for a limited time.

title: Study finds hundreds of people in Indonesia legally named after Naruto, Inuyasha, other anime stars
description: Anime’s growing international popularity is affecting name choices overseas. content:
Anime’s growing international popularity is affecting name choices overseas.

Popular storytelling tropes and traditions mean there’s often a degree of overlap among anime protagonists, but the characters that leave the deepest impressions tend to bring their traits together in some singular way that makes them stand out from the pack. So while, for example, anime has plenty of hot-blooded martial artist heroes, there’s only one Naruto, right?

Except, actually, in Indonesia, there are well over 100 Narutos. And no, this isn’t the result of somehow amplifying the power of bunshin/shadow cloning techniques, but part of a trend of actual people in Indonesia having the name of anime characters.

Earlier this month, Indonesia’s Directorate General of Population and Civil Registration (a.k.a. Dukcapil), part of the Ministry of Home Affairs, released its latest census data and found a surprising number of residents whose names clearly come from the anime/manga world. The most common anime name among the people of Indonesia is Uzumaki, with 190 people using Naruto’s surname as their name, while another 157 Indonesian residents are named Naruto. Hailing from the same series, the Dukcapil found 158 Sasukes and 152 Uchihas, creating totals of 347 people who owe their name to “Naruto Uzumaki” and 310 to “Sasuke Uchiha.” The census also turned up 60 people named after Boruto, Naruto’s son and star of his own sequel spinoff.

Doraemon also had a strong showing for inspiring names, with 181 people named Nobita, after the series’ lead human character. There are also 16 people in Indonesia named Doraemon, and another 8 share the name of Nobita’s wealthy associate Suneo.

Pirate saga One Piece’s popularity has resulted in 79 people named Luffy and 37 named Usopp. 65 people are named Shinchan, as in the titular tyke of Crayon Shin-chan, and Indonesia is also home to 23 people named Inuyasha.

To be clear, these tallies aren’t for people who use the anime character names as a professional name, nickname, or alias. The census counted official, legally registered names, meaning that any passports, driver’s licenses, or other official forms of ID issued to these people really will list their name as “Naruto” or “Inuyasha.”

The publicly released census data doesn’t seem to account for whether or not the people with these names are native Indonesians, but it’s unlikely that many of them are ethnically Japanese foreign residents. Naruto isn’t really a name that’s used in Japan, and Uzumaki is an incredibly rare family name, with estimates that there are fewer than a dozen Uzumakis in all of Japan. Sasuke is an actual given name, but one that’s very old-fashioned (we’re talking “immediately calls up images of ninja from hundreds of years ago” old-fashioned), and Uchiha doesn’t appear to be an actual surname name. The closest name out of those listed above that you’d be likely find an actual Japanese person with would be “Shin,” but even then, no Japanese person would make the affectionately diminutive suffix “-chan” part of their legal name.

Taking all that into consideration, it appears that these names really are the result of anime’s popularity in Indonesia, and with the medium’s global fanbase continuing to grow, we might be seeing even more anime names in the real world in years to come.

Source: Jiji, Yomiuri Shimbun, International Business Times, Myoji Yurai.net (1, 2)

title: Starbucks releases tear-jerking new video inspired by heartwarming encounters in Japanese stores
description: A beautiful homage to the true stories of customers and staff at Starbucks Japan. It’s been 30 years since Starbucks opened in Japan, and since then the chain has grown to include 2,100 stores across all 47 prefectures, with approximately 60,000 staff serving nearly 1 million customers every day. content:
A beautiful homage to the true stories of customers and staff at Starbucks Japan.

It’s been 30 years since Starbucks opened in Japan, and since then the chain has grown to include 2,100 stores across all 47 prefectures, with approximately 60,000 staff serving nearly 1 million customers every day.

Those are big numbers for a 30-year-old business, and to celebrate these three decades in Japan, the chain has released a tear-jerking new video that looks back at the many small moments and connections that have taken place at its stores over the years.

Starbucks says around 3 billion “hellos” and “thank yous” have been exchanged between customers and employees across its stores, and this new video pays homage to those exchanges, depicting moments of happiness and sadness that Starbucks learned about through interviews with staff and stories and comments submitted by customers.

Titled “Starbucks 30th Anniversary Brand Movie”, the video was released on 12 August, and displays a distinctive hand-crafted style inspired by the handwritten chalkboards associated with Starbucks stores.

▼ Take a look at the video below, and remember to keep some tissues handy!

From a daughter who grows up all too fast before her father’s eyes to the student who fails her entrance exam, and the elderly couple who are no longer able to enjoy each other’s company at Starbucks, this video really knows how to pull on the heartstrings. The message the chain wants to convey through the video is that Starbucks staff are always looking out for their customers, supporting them with smiles… and a little something to drink.

Helping to make the tears flow is an original song by singer-songwriter Anri Kumaki. Kumaki composed the music and provided the vocals while director Shinya Nakajima (a recipient of many awards including the Cannes Lions Grand Prix) wrote the lyrics based on the stories he heard while working on the project.

▼ Anri Kumaki

▼ Shinya Nakajima

Providing the art is award-winning art director Hidehito Yagi and his team, who spent every day drawing as part of what he described as a challenging but enjoyable process.

▼ Hidehito Yagi

▼ You can see both directors working on the project in the behind-the-scenes making-of video below.

So next time you step into a Starbucks in Japan, take heart in knowing that your story helps to contribute to the history of the chain. Whether you’re there for a happy occasion or to seek out some solace on a tough day, Starbucks wants all its customers to know that their stories, however small, are part of the story of Starbucks Japan.

title: Japanese airlines set to cut fuel surcharges for international flights in September and October
description: Flights to Japan are about to get cheaper for overseas tourists. With the yen recently reaching historically weak lows, Japan has become an increasingly affordable destination for many overseas tourists. Now, visitors to Japan can have even more cash in their back pocket as ANA and JAL are set to reduce their fuel surcharges for […]
content:
Flights to Japan are about to get cheaper for overseas tourists.

With the yen recently reaching historically weak lows, Japan has become an increasingly affordable destination for many overseas tourists. Now, visitors to Japan can have even more cash in their back pocket as ANA and JAL are set to reduce their fuel surcharges for international flights.

The two major Japanese airlines are expected to lower their fuel surcharges for tickets purchased in September and October, following several months of exceptionally high fees. These surcharges are typically added to international airfares to help airlines cover fluctuations in aviation fuel prices, and ANA and JAL revise their surcharges every two months, with the amount determined by fuel prices over the preceding two months.

The fluctuating prices can make a substantial difference to the price of airfares for passengers, as the surcharge is worked into the cost of the plane ticket. Fuel surcharges for ANA and JAL flights between Japan and Europe, North America, the Middle East and Oceania, rose to a record 65,000 yen (US$433) for tickets issued in July and August, up from 56,000 yen in May and June and 31,900 yen in March and April.

The incredibly high fees are largely due to a surge in aviation fuel prices following unrest in the Middle East, with the sharp increase eventually impacting the airlines’ surcharge calculations. The Japanese government’s emergency subsidy for aviation fuel, introduced in response to the Middle East situation, has now helped to ease costs, allowing the airlines to reduce charges for September and October.

While JAL is yet to release its official list of fuel surcharges for tickets issued from September through October, it has historically been on par with ANA, which updated its list of upcoming surcharges on 12 August. According to the update, for travellers flying between Japan and Europe, North America, the Middle East and Oceania, ANA’s surcharge will fall from 65,000 yen to 55,000 yen per person each way. That’s a saving of 10,000 yen each way, or 20,000 yen for a return trip.

Travellers from other parts of the world will also pay less, with surcharges on flights between Japan and Hawaii, India and Indonesia dropping from 40,400 yen to 35,800 yen, while flights to Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, Myanmar and Cambodia will fall from 33,500 yen to 27,300 yen. Flights to South Korea will be 900 yen cheaper at 6,500 yen, and flights to China and other destinations will be 1,100 yen cheaper at 14,300 yen.

As for other airlines, it’s too early to say whether they will also lower their fees. Fuel surcharges are set independently by each airline, so a reduction by ANA and JAL doesn’t necessarily indicate that other carriers will lower their own surcharges.

The new rates for ANA, and JAL if they follow suit as expected, are the cheapest they’ve been since 1 May. So if you’re thinking of booking a flight to Japan, you may want to hold off until 1 September, when the new fuel surcharges come into effect for tickets purchased from 1 September through 31 October.

Source: ANA, Nikkei, FNN via Yahoo! News Japan, Asahi Shimbun via Yahoo! News Japan

title: Delta Airlines adds first nonstop flight between Japan’s Narita Airport and U.S. in seven years
description: After a seven-year absence, Delta is ready for daily flights from its west coast hub to the Tokyo-area international airport. A lot has changed in the Japan travel sphere in the past seven years. After one of the longest international tourism shutdowns of any nation during the pandemic, worldwide interest in Japan’s pop culture, cuisine, […]
content:
After a seven-year absence, Delta is ready for daily flights from its west coast hub to the Tokyo-area international airport.

A lot has changed in the Japan travel sphere in the past seven years. After one of the longest international tourism shutdowns of any nation during the pandemic, worldwide interest in Japan’s pop culture, cuisine, and photogenic landscapes/cityscapes is soaring at the same time that the value of the yen is plummeting. So with Japan having never before been such an in-demand and affordable destination for travelers from overseas, Delta is finally ready to start flying directly again from the U.S. to one of Japan’s largest international airports.

2019 was the last time that Delta flew directly from the U.S. to Narita, one of the Tokyo area’s two international airports. Since then, all Delta flights connecting Narita and the U.S. have required at least one layover. Come next spring, though, Delta will be reinstating daily direct flights between Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, the airline’s primary west coast hub, and Narita.

The flights will depart from Seattle at 1:35 p.m. and, as a result of crossing the international date line, arrive at Narita at 4:20 p.m. the following day. Headed back the other way across the Pacific, flights will take off from Narita at 6:40 p.m. and land in Seattle at noon of the same calendar date. Narita Airport claims that the Narita-Seattle route will be the shortest air travel path between Japan and the continental United States.

The route will be serviced by an Airbus A330-900neo aircraft with a capacity of 281 passengers, with 29 business-class, 28 Premium Economy, 56 Delta Comfort, and 168 Delta Main (i.e. standard economy) seats.

The first flight on the route will be a Seattle departure on March 27, 2027.

content:
Sanrio’s kaiju crossover gives one cute character two extra heads, plus gives one character often overlooked in Japan some time in the spotlight.

Godzilla and Hello Kitty are on the highest tier of international stardom for Japanese pop culture icons. Long before the current global otaku and kawaii culture booms, the kaiju king and Sanrio queen were winning the hearts of fans far beyond their home country

So it’s understandable that McDonald’s America would be very happy to have either of them as a promotional partner. The burger chain is going one step farther, though, and instead of just Godzilla Happy Meals or Hello Kitty Happy Meals, they’re going to be offering Happy Meals with Godzilla and Hello Kitty together!

cosplaying right into our hearts. Hello Kitty and Friends x Godzilla Happy Meal out 8.18. pic.twitter.com/toTfyzcQ3k

— McDonald's (@McDonalds) August 12, 2026

Arriving later this month are the brand-new Hello Kitty and Friends x Godzilla Happy Meals, which McDonald’s is billing as “cute meets kaiju.” The toys will consist of eight different team-ups between a Sanrio character and a giant monster, with the pairings being:
● Hello Kitty x Godzilla
● Kuromi x Mechagodzilla
● My Melody x Mothra
● Pompompurin x Gigan
● Cinnamoroll x Destoroyah
● Badtz-Maru x Rodan
● Kero Kero Keroppi x King Ghidorah
● Chococat x Space Godzilla

There seems to be some fun logic between some of those team-ups, such as the gentle and considerate My Melody being paired with motherly Mothra, the always-assertive Kuromi with hubris-born Mechagodzilla, and the repeating aspect of Kero Kero Keroppi’s name dovetailing with the three-headed anatomy of King Ghidorah. Chococat’s inclusion in the lineup might seem like a surprise, but while the character often gets lost in the Sanrio swarm in Japan, he placed third among U.S. voters in this year’s Sanrio Character Poll, so his apparently sizable fandom in the States likely played a role in getting him a spot in the collaboration.

McDonald’s says that these characters will be “cosplaying right into our hearts,” implying that these are meant to be kigurumi/one-piece costumes of kaiju that the Sanrio characters are wearing. However, Keroppi Ghidorah having three heads suggests the possibility that the Sanrio characters are fusing with their partner kaiju, and this video of Kitty Godzilla approaching a defenseless Happy Meal freighter has an unmistakably sinister tone to it that makes one wonder if she’s becoming influenced by the kaiju’s destructive tendencies.

View this post on Instagram

▼ Will shipping companies need to summon Archfiend Hello Kitty to protect their cargo from this new threat?

The Hello Kitty and Friends x Godzilla Happy Meals are scheduled to go on sale at U.S. McDonald’s locations on August 18, with no word yet as to whether they’ll be available in Japan.

title: The Japanese city where ordering grilled chicken doesn’t guarantee you’ll actually get chicken
description: Just a short train ride from Tokyo and you’ll be left addicted to delicious skewers slathered in a fiery miso sauce. Japan has a lot of lists of “Three Great…”, from beautiful sceneries to shrines at the bottom of a flight of stairs, but there is also a list for yakitori (literally “grilled chicken”). These […]
content:
Just a short train ride from Tokyo and you’ll be left addicted to delicious skewers slathered in a fiery miso sauce.

Japan has a lot of lists of “Three Great…”, from beautiful sceneries to shrines at the bottom of a flight of stairs, but there is also a list for yakitori (literally “grilled chicken”). These humble skewers of chicken meat, often found at festivals, roadside stalls, or at pubs, may not be your first thought for ranking a food nationally, but there are three cities in the country that are known to outshine the rest: Muroran in Hokkaido, Imabari in Ehime, and Higashimatsuyama in Saitama. Although one of them has a surprising twist in that they are not made from chicken at all.

With both Hokkaido and Ehime being on different islands to Tokyo, they’re not exactly somewhere you can pop over in order to sample their delights, but Saitama is different. Just a short train ride from the capital on the Tobu Tojo line, you’ll soon come to the city of Higashimatsuyama, which stands out for its unique culinary identity rooted in postwar history.

▼ Higashimatsuyama Station Building

The tradition began in 1956, when the founder of the yakitori store Daimatsuya opened a shop in the area. At the time, pork kashira (meat from a pig’s temple and cheek) was rarely utilized in Japanese cooking, but by grilling this tender yet chewy pork and pairing it with a spicy miso sauce, it proved to be a massive hit with the locals. The original owner shared the kashira recipe with local vendors, establishing this unique dish as a core element of local food culture.

▼ Heading to Saitamaya‘s Higashimatsuyama Ekimae store, we were excited to finally give it a try for ourselves.

Looking at the menu, three types of lunch sets were available, and while we were also curious about the Secret Miso Fried Chicken Set, we couldn’t exactly satisfy ourselves with fried chicken after coming all of this way.

So, we ordered the Higashimatsuyama specialty Yakitori-ju Set, costing 1,200 yen (US$7.54). To go along with it, we also splurged on a lunch drink, costing an extra 100 yen, and the Gokutoro Liver (680 yen) we spotted on the menu posted on the wall; it just looked so delicious we couldn’t help ourselves.

▼ The first to arrive was the liver, looking fresh and faintly tinged with pink.

Throwing a bite into our mouth, it had a sublime melt-in-your-mouth texture that is to be expected of something called “toro” (the Japanese culinary term for something rich and tender).

Then came the Yakitori-ju, a heavy box set that comes with miso soup, pickles, and a small side dish. There are four skewers: Kashira, Negima (chicken and green onion), Tsukune (chicken meatballs), and Eggplant.

While the Negima, Tsukune, and Eggplant looked positively delectable, it was the Kashira that we were most interested in sinking our teeth into.

The meat offers a firm texture, satisfying chew, and rich umami that differs completely from chicken, complemented by the fiery punch of the miso sauce for an addictive combination.

Unlike traditional local eateries, where kashira skewers are served continuously until diners ask the chef to stop, more modern establishments like Saitamaya offer standard menu ordering, so if you’re looking to try some kashira for yourselves, you’ll need to plan in advance what sort of experience you’re looking for. Now, we just need to find an excuse to make our way to Hokkaido and Ehime.

title: This beautiful Okinawa beach gives you the best of both worlds when visiting the prefecture [Pics]
description: Minnajima combines remote-island beauty with main-island-stay convenience. It’s a long way to Okinawa from most parts of the rest of Japan. Getting there from Tokyo, for example, requires you to first go to Haneda Airport, get through all your check-in procedures, fly for about two and a half hours to Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, and […]
content:
Minnajima combines remote-island beauty with main-island-stay convenience.

It’s a long way to Okinawa from most parts of the rest of Japan. Getting there from Tokyo, for example, requires you to first go to Haneda Airport, get through all your check-in procedures, fly for about two and a half hours to Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, and then, after you land, make your way to the beach.

This had us in a bit of a quandary on our recent trip to Okinawa. The prefecture’s best beaches are on its outer islands, but getting to them tacks yet another time and energy-consuming segment onto the total journey, so we were thinking of maybe just making do with the coastal options on Okinawa’s main island, which are still nicer than the beaches in most other parts of Japan.

But then we took another look at the map and noticed Minnajima Island.

▼ Minnajima Island

Minnajima is only about 15 minutes by boat from Toguchi Port in the town of Motobu on Okinawa’s main island. We heard, though, that it’s in a whole other class in terms of beach beauty, and so we headed to the port to catch a 10:30 a.m. ferry to see the place for ourselves.

We booked our tickets as part of a package through marine sports/tour company Mermaid, paying 4,500 yen (US$29) for round-trip ferry fare, lunch, and beach umbrella rental, all of which turned out to be things we were happy to have sorted out ahead of time. The same tour is priced at 3,500 yen for kids ages 6 to 11 and 500 yen for children 5 and younger (although that youngest age bracket doesn’t include lunch).

Almost every seat on the ferry was full, but the ship departed right on schedule, and as we drew closer to the Minnajima dock…

…the ocean transitioned to a brilliant blue. The color was so dazzling it reminded us of a tropical cocktail, and not only was the water’s hue breathtaking, but its clarity was too.

At the beach, the tour’s partner staff asked us where we’d like our beach umbrellas set up, and then planted them in the sand for us.

Even if you’re not ordinarily the sort of person who uses a parasol at the beach, we’d recommend one here. While there are lockers and shower facilities, there aren’t really any shade-providing structures or vegetation. Without an umbrella, you’re going to be in direct sunlight pretty much nonstop, and the sunlight is definitely strong here in midsummer.

And again, we can’t stress enough how incredible the water is here. Sometimes when looking at photos posted online of Okinawa beaches, it’s hard to imagine there isn’t some serious filter and color-processing going on, but this really is how Minnajima looks.

As for why booking a package day-trip that includes lunch is a smart idea, there are very few restaurant options on the island, and if you bring your own food, you’ll have to store and carry home all of your own trash, as there are no trash receptacles at the beach. Our package provided us with Okinawa soba noodles at a cafe up the street from the beach, and even the walk there featured great scenery, such as a field of sugarcane.

▼ Our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko and his daughter having lunch after hitting the beach

Our boat back to the main island left at 3:30 p.m., and while it might have been nice to stay longer and take the 4:30 ferry instead, we still got to spend close to five hours on Minnajima, and it was time very well spent.

In a way, Minnajima represents the best of both worlds when traveling in Okinawa. Obviously, it’s not deserted during the peak summer travel season, but it was significantly less crowded than the main island’s major beaches. It lets you experience a more unique, and beautiful, part of Okinawa Prefecture’s coastline, but its day-trip-doable status still lets you have the convenience, larger selection of hotels, and larger amount of free time that comes from staying on the main island. Just be sure, if you’re headed to Okinawa, to watch out for the new luggage check-in rules at Haneda Airport.

title: Shinto shrine in downtown Tokyo announces cosplay ban
description: No more cosplaying on shrine grounds, please, says Yasukuni. There’s more to consider than just costuming, makeup, and posing when taking cosplay photos. If you want a really convincing shot, you’re going to need a good background too. Thankfully, for those cosplaying as characters whose outfits draw inspiration from samurai, ninja, yokai, or other symbols […]
content:
No more cosplaying on shrine grounds, please, says Yasukuni.

There’s more to consider than just costuming, makeup, and posing when taking cosplay photos. If you want a really convincing shot, you’re going to need a good background too. Thankfully, for those cosplaying as characters whose outfits draw inspiration from samurai, ninja, yokai, or other symbols of traditional Japanese folklore, there are plenty of places in Japan with classical aesthetics. However, one of Tokyo’s most prominent Shinto shrines, Yasukuni Shrine, has updated its visitor policies and now expressly bans cosplaying on its premises.

According to the statement posted to Yasukuni’s official website on August 7, the cosplay ban is being put into place to help maintain the “solemn” and “sacred” atmosphere of the shrine grounds. That might sound heavy-handed in contrast to the generally casual vibe at many other shrines in Japan, but Yasukuni is in a uniquely complex position because of the shrine’s purpose.

Yasukuni Shrine was built in 1869 to enshrine members of Japan’s modern (i.e. post-feudal era) armed forces. This now includes many members of the Japanese Imperial Army and Navy who fought in World War II. As such, Yasukuni often finds itself at the center of controversies if politicians, celebrities, or other prominent figures visit the shrine, with especially strong criticism coming from China, Korea, or other victims of Japanese aggression in World War II. Meanwhile, pointedly or explicitly avoiding visiting Yasukuni can be seen by some as disrespectful to those who gave their lives in service of the country. Further complicating the situation is that Yasukuni enshrines some 2.4 million souls, of which 1,066 are convicted war criminals, but casting them out would be incongruent with the shrine’s intended purpose of spiritual salvation.

All of which is to say that it’s understandable that Yasukuni probably doesn’t want to be seen as doing anything to cultivate an image that it’s a “cool” or “fun” place, and would prefer to maintain an atmosphere with a seriousness befitting the weight of the shrine’s purpose, which brings us back to the statement posted to its website.

Requests regarding attire on the shrine grounds

Yasukuni Shrine is a solemn and sacred site that exists to comfort and enshrine the souls of the war dead who gave their precious lives for Japan. So that all visitors may offer their sincere prayers in a tranquil environment, we ask for your cooperation with the following:

● The wearing of cosplay outfits on shrine grounds is prohibited.
● The wearing of military uniforms (military attire, military equipment, etc.) on shrine grounds is prohibited.

The mention of “military uniforms” adds another layer to the new policy, and the exact terminology is especially significant. Yasukuni Shrine’s statement refers to gunsou and gunpuku, which translate literally to “military outfits” and “military clothing.” However, the Japan Self-Defense Forces do not use either word to refer to the official attire of JSDF personnel, and instead use seifuku, which simply means “uniform,” with no military-related linguistic connotation. As a result, the words gunsou and gunpuku usually evoke thoughts of Japanese military uniforms from before the JSDF’s founding.

Taking all of that into account, it would seem that Yasukuni Shrine’s new policy does not prohibit members of the JSDF from visiting the shrine in dress uniform. However, the explicit gunsou/gunpuku ban does prohibit someone from visiting while dressed in an Imperial Japanese Army or Navy uniform, and it would apply both to cosplayers trying to exploit a loophole by trying to argue that a uniform is not a costume as well as far-right wingers trying to use the shrine as a stage to trumpet their nostalgia for Japan’s aggressively militaristic past.

This is also a good opportunity to remember that cosplaying rules can vary widely from shrine to shrine, and on the opposite end of the spectrum from Yasukuni are shrines that have hosted official cosplay events. At all times, though, it’s important to remember that these are first and foremost places of religious and cultural importance, and so if you are hoping to cosplay at a shrine, it’s probably best to check their website or contact the shrine ahead of time to confirm what their policy is.

title: Tokyo sweets store has a “350% Pudding Soft Serve”, and people are going wild for it
description: Is this ice cream dessert worth the hype? If you’re looking for an area of Tokyo where you can enjoy a wide variety of fancy sweets, then Ginza needs to be on your list. Right now there’s even more reason to visit the ritzy neighbourhood, because sweet tooths on social media in Japan have been […]
content:
Is this ice cream dessert worth the hype?

If you’re looking for an area of Tokyo where you can enjoy a wide variety of fancy sweets, then Ginza needs to be on your list. Right now there’s even more reason to visit the ritzy neighbourhood, because sweet tooths on social media in Japan have been raving about something called the “350% Pudding Soft Serve”.

Pudding, or “purin” as it’s known in Japanese, is like a Japanese custard pudding or creme caramel. Though it sometimes makes an appearance as a soft serve ice cream flavour, we’d never heard of a “350% Pudding Soft Serve” before, so we took the train to Ginza to find out what it was all about.

Located on the first floor of Exitmelsa, not far from the Ginza 4-chome intersection, we found the viral dessert at Purin Kenkyujo (“Pudding Lab“).

Purin Kenkyujo describes itself as a high-end pudding specialty shop that uses quality ingredients for premium flavour. It operates primarily as an online business, with products made to order, but it has one physical store, here in Ginza.

At this store, you can find three types of purin soft serve, or “soft cream”, on the menu: “100%”, “150%”, and “350%”.

▼ Percentages are an unusual way to sell a dessert.

Looking at the descriptions for each, we discovered that the 100% Pudding Soft Serve (1,080 yen [US$6.82]) was described as “a sweet made by squeezing pudding that has been frozen at minus-eight degrees Celsius (minus-17.6 degrees Fahrenheit) into the form of soft-serve ice cream.”

The 150% is the “100% Pudding Soft Serve” with one pudding added as a topping (1,296 yen), while the “350%” contains the “100% Pudding Soft Serve” with a whopping five additional puddings. The price for the 350% is 1,836 yen (US$11.60).

▼ Naturally, we went for the “350% Pudding Soft-Serve”, which staff prepared right in front of us.

▼ It looked adorable, with its cluster of small puddings sitting on top.

▼ You can choose two caramel sauces with your order, and the bitter one was particularly delicious.

The purin were delectably soft and jiggly, filled with the rich custard flavour that makes the dessert so popular. In between bites of purin, we were able to enjoy spoonfuls of purin-flavoured soft serve, giving us two ways to enjoy the sweet treat.

Though this dessert sits on the pricey end of the purin spectrum, considering that Ginza is one of the poshest districts in all of Tokyo, with prices to match, and Purin Kenkyujo sells puddings that can cost up to 5,400 yen ($34.12), this isn’t a bad deal for a quality sweet in Tokyo.

Is it worth the hype and calories? Well, for dessert lovers, absolutely. It’s moreish, decadent, and a delicious way to overload on pudding. If you’re simply in it for the ‘Gram, then it’ll definitely get you noticed on social media, so in our opinion it’s a win-win for all types of sweet tooths, and worth the trip to Ginza to try it.

title: Japanese figure skating star Yuzuru Hanyu and Winne-the-Pooh announce crossover merch line [Pics]
description: Pooh Shower tradition inspires over 100 crossover items. content:
Pooh Shower tradition inspires over 100 crossover items.

Japan has tons of cool character merch, and the fun gets doubled when its part of a crossover, like when Hello Kitty teams up with the cast of Sesame Street, Yu-Gi-Oh, or Evangelion. Japan’s newest collaboration, though, isn’t between two fictional characters, but between one of Disney’s most beloved icons and one of the country’s biggest sports heroes.

Yuzuru Hanyu secured his status as Japan’s most celebrated male figure skater with back-to-back gold medals at the 2014 and 2018 Olympics. Before he was associated with the shine of Olympic gold, though, he was connected to bright yellow bear Winnie-the-Pooh. As far back as 2010, people started noticing that Hanyu had a Winnie-the-Pooh plushie-style tissue box rinkside during practices and competitions, and it became tradition for fans to shower the ice with stuffed animals of the character following his performances.

This October 14 will be the 100th anniversary of the release of the original Winnie-the-Pooh children’s book, and to celebrate, a series of Yuzuru Hanyu/Winnie-the-Pooh popup shops will be offering crossover merch of the pair.

Called Shower of Heart, evoking thoughts of the “Pooh Shower,” as fans have come to call the after-skate showering of gifts onto the ice, the merchandise line will consist of over 100 exclusive items. So far, the organizers have revealed that there’ll be acrylic standees…

…key holders/bag straps…

…and a special Winnie-the-Pooh plushie with an extra-classy shimmery-fabric shirt.

▼ Pooh Bear is, however, apparently still saying “Nah, I’m good” regarding pants.

The Shower of Heart popup store tour starts in Tokyo at Shibuya Tsutaya from October 2 to 30, then heads to Kyoto’s Takashimaya S.C. (November 3-15), Nagoya’s JR Nagoya Takashimaya (November 18-29), Okayama’s Okayama Takashimaya (January 8-19), Fukuoka’s Hakata Hankyu (April 21-May 10), and, finally Sendai’s Fujisaki department store (May 27-June 8).

title: Beautiful off-the-beaten-path spot near samurai castle in rural Japan looks like a Monet painting
description: Here’s today’s reason not to skip Gifu in your Japan travel plans. As Japan becomes an increasingly popular destination for international travelers, there’s also a growing sense that some of the country’s most famous prefectures are becoming so crowded that their appeal is starting to fade. At the same time, this means there’s value in […]
content:
Here’s today’s reason not to skip Gifu in your Japan travel plans.

As Japan becomes an increasingly popular destination for international travelers, there’s also a growing sense that some of the country’s most famous prefectures are becoming so crowded that their appeal is starting to fade. At the same time, this means there’s value in taking the time to search for cool places that aren’t on the typical Japan travel itinerary, and doing that today once again brings us to Gifu Prefecture.

We recently visited the Enbaragawa River, a beautiful waterway in Gifu’s Yamagata City. Today, we’re heading further south in Gifu, closer to the border with Aichi Prefecture, for a stop in the town of Kakamigahara.

As with the Enbaragawa River, we’re not here for a glitzy luxury travel hot spot, but a quiet place of tranquil beauty. And while it might not immediately seem like there’s such a place to be found on this narrow strip of rural backroad, right about where you spot this vinyl-sided greenhouse…

…if you cross over to the other side of the street you’ll find a crystalline waterway that’s beautiful enough to be a painting.

We’re not the only ones who feel that way, either. Among those who know about this place, it’s often referred to as being a real-life Monet pond because of how much it looks like it could be one of the works of the Impressionist artist.

The water here is so clear that you can see down to every little pebble at the bottom, and when fish swim, it can play tricks on your eyes and make you think for a second that they’re floating in the air.

This stream is actually part of the Hashima Irrigation Canal, and it owes its clarity in part to an annual dose of oyster shells placed in it to naturally absorb and filter out impurities from the water.

As a result, the koi that live in the canal looked very happy on the day we visited, and presented us with a parade of fish in dazzling gold, bright white, and sleek black.

We were especially impressed when this aquatic quintet came swimming by in formation, as if they were showing off since they saw we had our camera out.

Since it’s an irrigation canal, the water here is always gently flowing, and not only does this create a gently soothing vibe, it also means that the way the light plays off the water is always subtly shifting. This means that every picture you snap is going to have its own unique feel to it, and even just sitting on the nearby bench and watching the canal is a unique mix of stimulation and relaxation.

▼ The section of the canal we visited

The town of Kakamigahara itself isn’t exactly bursting with other sightseeing spots, but the canal isn’t too far from the Kisogawa Lookout Point, which has nice views of the surrounding area…

▼ Route from Hashima Irrigation Canal to Kisogawa Lookout Point

…and it’s also just a quick hop across the river to Inuyama Castle, which features one of Japan’s oldest original samurai stronghold towers.

▼ Route from Hashima Irrigation Canal to Inuyama Castle

So yes, even if you missed out on this year’s Holy Fungus Mud Volleyball tournament, Gifu is still worth a visit.

title: Wagyu ramen for foreign tourists appears in Kabukicho, with a very high price tag
description: What makes this bowl of noodles cost around twice as much as a regular ramen, and is it worth it? Ever since the pandemic eased, inbound tourism has been booming in Japan, with record numbers of overseas visitors arriving in the country. In fact, it’s hard to walk through almost any area of central Tokyo […]
content:
What makes this bowl of noodles cost around twice as much as a regular ramen, and is it worth it?

Ever since the pandemic eased, inbound tourism has been booming in Japan, with record numbers of overseas visitors arriving in the country. In fact, it’s hard to walk through almost any area of central Tokyo without passing a visitor from overseas, and for many businesses that’s seen as a good thing, especially as the weak yen gives them greater spending power than local customers.

In an attempt to appeal to these overseas customers, you can now see multilingual posters and products aimed at tourists all over the city. Our reporter P.K. Sanjun recently came across one such poster outside the Kabukicho branch of ramen chain Mita Seimenjo, where the words “WAGYU RAMEN” in large font immediately caught his eye.

▼ With no Japanese writing on the poster whatsoever, this was clearly a menu item that was marketed towards foreign tourists.

Mita Seimenjo might not have the same level of instant brand recognition amongst foreign visitors compared to rival chains, but locals know it for its rich seafood-and-pork-bone broth and thick, chewy noodles. P.K. himself says it’s probably most famous for its tsukemen (dipping noodles), and he has a lot of praise for its excellent karaage (fried chicken) too.

With over 50 branches, mainly located around Tokyo, P.K. has visited his fair share of Mita Seimenjos but not once had he seen the “WAGYU RAMEN” poster before. After running a search for it online, he couldn’t find any mention of it on the chain’s official website, leading him to believe it must be a Kabukicho branch exclusive.

Never one to pass up an opportunity to try a new ramen, P.K. stepped inside the store and ordered it, while wincing slightly at the 2,380 yen (US$16) expenditure, which is around twice the cost of the tsukemen he normally orders at the chain. Though local customers would balk at such a price tag, the chain even offers an extra slice of A5 Wagyu for 1,480 yen, making it a very expensive topping.

When his order arrived, it certainly looked delicious – a generous slice of Wagyu beef dominated the top of the bowl, crowned with a raw egg yolk for an extra touch of luxury.

On the side, as if to avoid stealing the spotlight from the beef, were spring onions and bamboo shoots, served separately on a small plate.

Taking a sip of the broth, it was exactly what he expected from Mita Seimenjo. The reliably delicious seafood-and-pork-bone broth paired perfectly with the smooth, chewy noodles, and he had to admit that at this point, it was an excellent ramen.

▼ Time to try the Wagyu.

Though he’d initially had his doubts, he needn’t have doubted the skills of Mita Seimenjo, because this was a fantastic slice of A5 beef. Beautifully marbled, it was incredibly rich, with a remarkable sweetness to the fat that had him wanting to jump up and do a happy wagyu dance.

Just when he thought things couldn’t get any more indulgent, he added the accompanying truffle into the broth and it immediately transformed the taste of the entire bowl, giving it an even richer, more luxurious flavour. In the end, the truffle left just as much of an impression on P.K. as the Wagyu itself.

▼ The truffle, and the raw egg, really elevated the soup.

After slurping up the final mouthful of broth, P.K. was pleased to discover that this wasn’t an expensive tourist gimmick. Rather than simply placing an expensive slice of Wagyu on top of a plain bowl of ramen, careful consideration had been given to the dish as a whole, balancing the flavours with quality ingredients that made the price feel surprisingly reasonable.

That said, if P.K. were to return, he’d probably opt for two bowls of the chain’s delicious tsukemen instead of one bowl of WAGYU RAMEN. However, from a tourist’s point-of-view, the chance to enjoy two of Japan’s most famous culinary exports, ramen and Wagyu beef, in a single bowl will likely be a temptation too hard to resist. So go ahead and indulge, as this is a food encounter you won’t regret, but keep in mind that the tsukemen is also worth a look-in, as that’s what locals really keep coming back for.

title: Did you know? Only one Beard Papa’s in all of eastern Japan sells soft serve in a cream puff
description: The legendary Japanese chain known for its heavenly cream puffs has only a handful of stores where you can pair pastry with an icy treat. content:
The legendary Japanese chain known for its heavenly cream puffs has only a handful of stores where you can pair pastry with an icy treat.

Japanese cream puff (“choux cream”) specialty store Beard Papa’s has got to be home to one of the best scents on this planet. Whether you’re strolling leisurely while shopping or rushing through a train station, you’ll know immediately when you’ve stumbled upon a store location by the heavenly aroma suddenly wafting everywhere around you in the air.

Despite being famous for its pastries, the chain began selling frozen custard soft serve ice cream at a select few of its locations several years ago, with the fourth and latest location in Aichi Prefecture being added to the lineup last July. However, while there are now locations in Osaka, Hyogo, and Aichi prefectures in western Japan, the store in Higashimatsuyama, Saitama Prefecture remains the only one in all of eastern Japan.

▼ This promotional visual at the Saitama store proclaims that the soft serve “can only be eaten here in all of eastern Japan.”

Saitama is easily accessible from the heart of Tokyo, so we decided to pay this branch a visit to enjoy its special menu item, eventually arriving at Tobu Railway’s Takasaka Station via the Tobu Tojo Line. This is the closest train station to the Peony Walk Higashimatsuyama shopping center where the branch is located. Even so, it’s still either a 20-minute walk or a 10-minute bus ride to get there. On this particular day, we elected to get some exercise in by walking since the heat was relatively low by Japanese summer standards.

Once there, it was easy to locate the store on the first floor of the mall. It looked just like any other Beard Papa’s location upon first glance…

…but there was a unique sign out front displaying its status as the only shop in the eastern Kanto region selling the custard soft serve. You can purchase a cup of it by itself for 330 yen (US$2.09) or as a “cookie choux soft serve” for 360 yen. 

While the frozen treat was definitely tempting on its own, it was a no-brain-freezer for us–we wanted to try it alongside the puff pastry that Beard Papa’s is famous for.

The tantalizing treat that was handed to us looked like it was in serious danger of a meltdown, so we got to work on it right away. Thank goodness the temperature wasn’t obscenely hot on this day or we couldn’t have imagined how quickly we’d be holding nothing but a soggy pastry shell.

Of course, we had to sacrifice a few seconds in order to document the impressive, undisturbed visuals.

The soft serve was luxuriously creamy and rich. It really hit the spot but also didn’t feel heavy inside the mouth.

The combination of soft serve and puff pastry base made for an exquisite pairing with intermingling smooth and flaky textures. We’re sure they would each taste divine on their own, but something about the two of them together seemed to elevate their respective flavors even more.

It’s already been a year since Beard Papa’s added its latest store selling the frozen custard soft serve, and we think they’re long overdue to add another. We know that you’re always busy adding delicious new menu items, Beard Papa’s, but we’d love for you to expand the ones that already exist, too!

title: Stray cats almost became classified as an invasive species in Japan but the change was overturned
description: This week, the Ministry of the Environment is caught between intensely divided public opinion on what’s truly best for cats vs. other species. Given Japan’s love for all things feline in the modern day, it’s easy to forget that the domestic cat isn’t actually native to the island nation. They were originally introduced during the […]
content:
This week, the Ministry of the Environment is caught between intensely divided public opinion on what’s truly best for cats vs. other species.

Given Japan’s love for all things feline in the modern day, it’s easy to forget that the domestic cat isn’t actually native to the island nation. They were originally introduced during the Heian period (794-1185) via trade ships as a way to deter rats from eating Buddhist scrolls and kept almost exclusively by nobility. It wasn’t until later eras that they became more widespread and grew immensely in population–at times having negative effects on the local ecosystem.

On August 4, Japan’s Ministry of the Environment announced its intent to withdraw a proposed revision that included stray cats–those that depend on humans for survival–on its list of invasive alien species causing damage to local ecosystems. Previously, only feral cats in the wild had been included on the list, and the Ministry was in the final stages of adding an entry for all domestic cats lumped together under their collective species name (Felis catus). However, the decision was met with a flood of public criticism that such a designation might result in pet house cats being unintentionally exterminated if they were to escape. Consequently, the Ministry reverted back to its previous classification of feral cats on the list.

▼ Even when they don’t have a clear owner, stray cats are hard to be seen by many as dangerous pests when they’re just so darn cute.

This year marks the first time that the list of invasive alien species is being revised in approximately 10 years. Despite holding no legally binding power, the list’s proposed revision for feline kind was intended to caution people not to let their house cats roam around outside unsupervised or to abandon them. As Japan has seen time and time again, invasive species such as the red-necked longhorn beetle can have devastating effects on the local environment.

▼ The Amami rabbit, an Endangered species that is endemic to only two of the Amami Islands in southern Japan, is one species threatened by stray cats.

Hirotaka Ishihara, the current Minister of the Environment, shared at a press conference on the same day that the proposed revision had the possibility of inviting misunderstandings such as that someone’s pet house cat would be put down if it escapes, also citing the high risk of unintended consequences that are unrelated to the list’s original objective. The list’s final revised policy was subsequently determined at an assembly of experts he convened on August 7, a move that is extremely unusual at that stage in the process.

Online reaction to the elimination of the proposed revision was largely met with negative backlash, with many net users upset at what they felt to be a step in the wrong direction:

“Even though prevention ≠ extermination…”
“Who’s going to protect the environment if not the Ministry of the Environment?!”
“Do they really have to withdraw the language out of fear it will be misunderstood? Can’t they just implement measures to prevent the language from being misinterpreted?”
“It feels like a governmental betrayal when a lot of us were finally raising awareness of the importance of keeping cats indoors.”
“So it’s OK when the raccoons or nutrias are being exterminated but it’s considered abuse when it comes to cats?”

It’s unclear how the government plans to tackle the prevalence of stray cats in certain parts of Japan, but there’s already proof of certain localities taking matters into their own hands, including Japan’s most famous “cat island,” Aoshima, which revealed that all of its stray cats will be gone in the very near future due to the population being too large for the small, aging human population to manage.

content:
Kiki’s Delivery Service steals the spotlight with exclusive plushies… and jewellery that would make Kiki jealous.

We all know that young witch Kiki is the star of Studio Ghibli’s 1989 film Kiki’s Delivery Service, but the titular character’s star power is often eclipsed by her black cat and familiar, Jiji.

Being the kind-hearted soul she is, Kiki likely wouldn’t be fazed by Jiji’s worldwide popularity – in fact, every time Ghibli specialty chain Donguri Kyowakoku releases a new line of merchandise related to the feline, we can imagine Kiki herself lining up with the rest of us to purchase the goods so she can proudly share her love for Jiji.

If Kiki were to jump out of the anime world and into the real one, both she and Jiji would likely be making a beeline for the store right now, because Donguri Kyowkoku has released a new plush toy in honour of…

▼ … JIji’s baby!

This is an unusual release for the chain, as the spotlight is usually set firmly on Jiji rather than his offspring, whom we only meet briefly in the closing credits of the film. This late introduction of Jiji’s children, whom he shares with girlfriend Lily, can leave viewers wondering what adventures they get up to next, and this new release gives us a way to answer that, as we can now pick this baby up to keep us company at home.

If Kiki and Jiji were able to see this plushie, they’d be cooing over the gorgeous details, with the large, youthful wide eyes and perky pink ears making it look like a younger version of JIji.

▼ Pair it with a Jiji plushie from the same chain and you get a charming family scene.

Called “Jiji’s Baby Plush Toy“, the soft plushie has a velour-like smooth texture that’s said to be so pleasant to touch you’ll want to keep petting it. Measuring 16 centimetres (6.3 inches) in height, the baby is priced at 3,300 yen (US$20.85).

As an added bonus, Donguri Kyowakoku has also added another unusual plushie to its lineup, by restocking the “Looks Just Like Jiji” plushie (2,750 yen).

As fans will know, this plushie recreates the one that appears in a wicker basket in the film, which looks uncannily like Jiji.

Kiki is tasked with delivering the toy as part of her delivery service, where it’s meant to be a gift for Ketto, but she ends up losing it.

This leads to a humorous sequence of events, where Jiji has to step in to pretend to be the plush toy, while Kiki’s friend Ursula sews the damaged plushie back together.

Those stitching details appear on the plush toy, making it seem like the real one from the world of Kiki’s Delivery Service.

The love for everything Jiji-related continues with the restock of a collection of jewellery in honour of the cat, and the Guchokipanya bakery where he and Kiki spend much of their time in the movie.

▼ This beautifully crafted jewellery line is called The Guchokipanya Bakery Series.

▼ Jiji’s love for jam is depicted in the “Jiji Clinging to a Jam Jar” necklace (2,970 yen).

In the “Jam Jar and Jiji” earrings (available in pierced and clip-on varieties for 2,970 yen per pair), the cat can be seen with a whole piece of bread in his mouth.

▼ The earrings let you dangle Jiji from one ear lobe…

▼ …and a jar of jam from the other.

All the items are so beautiful that Kiki herself would want to buy them all, but as always they are only being produced in limited quantities so you’ll want to step into a Donguri Kyowakoku store or purchase them online (links below) before they sell out.

title: Over 1,400 cities in Japan see foreign population rise, total populations drop in new statistics
description: Japan’s foreign population is growing in both size and proportion, ministry study shows. Japan’s population has been shrinking since 2010, but in recent years the country has seen a significant growth in its number of foreign residents. Showing just how starkly the sizes of Japan’s natural-born and foreign demographics are moving in opposite directions, newly […]
content:
Japan’s foreign population is growing in both size and proportion, ministry study shows.

Japan’s population has been shrinking since 2010, but in recent years the country has seen a significant growth in its number of foreign residents. Showing just how starkly the sizes of Japan’s natural-born and foreign demographics are moving in opposite directions, newly released data from the Japanese government’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications shows that between January 1 of 2025 and 2026, there were 1,436 municipalities in Japan where the total population declined, but the number of foreign residents increased.

The biggest growth in foreign resident population took place in the city of Osaka, where the foreign population grew by 25,056 people during the year. Osaka was followed by Yokohama (11,056 more foreign residents than the previous year), Nagoya (10,091 more foreign residents), Kyoto (6,483 more foreign residents), and Kawaguchi, in Saitama Prefecture (5,629 more foreign residents).

● Largest increases in foreign residents between January 1, 2025 and January 1, 2026
1. Osaka: 25,056
2. Yokohama: 11,056
3. Nagoya: 10,091
4. Kyoto: 6,483
5. Kawaguchi: 5,629
6. Kobe: 5,033
7. Tokyo, Edogawa Ward: 4,839
8. Chiba City: 4,086
9. Tokyo, Shinjuku Ward: 3,260
10. Sapporo: 3,216

It might seem odd that Tokyo doesn’t show up until seventh place on the list, but that’s due to a quirk in how the data was collected and presented. The Tokyo Metropolis is made up of a large number of officially designated wards and cities, and each of these was counted separately by the ministry. 10 Tokyo wards/cities were among the top 100 municipalities in foreign population growth, with a total increase of 22,118 residents among them, which would have put Tokyo in second place on the list, and perhaps even first if the foreign population increase for every part of the metropolis were pooled.

● Largest increases in foreign residents between January 1, 2025 and January 1, 2026
7. Tokyo, Edogawa Ward: 4,839

Meanwhile, in all of the top-10 municipalities for foreign resident growth, the Japanese population decreased, and in six of the top 10, the number of new foreign residents was actually larger than the decrease in Japanese residents, resulting in a net gain in population.

● Osaka: 19,865 more new foreign residents than reduced Japanese residents
● Nagoya: 7,717 more new foreign residents
● Kawaguchi: 1,068 more new foreign residents
● Tokyo, Edogawa Ward: 4,844 more new foreign residents
● Chiba City: 2,709 more new foreign residents
● Tokyo, Shinjuku Ward: 2,408 more new foreign residents

It should be pointed out that municipalities’ increases in foreign residents were not solely a result of increased immigration to Japan during the year. Preexisting foreign residents of Japan moving into a new municipality were also part of the tallies, as were births of children born to foreign residents (as Japan does not have a system of birth right citizenship).

However, the increase from a preexisting foreign resident moving to a new city would also be reflected as a decrease in the foreign population in the city they moved out of, and with so many of Japan’s major population centers seeing large growths in foreign population at the same time, the increases can’t be the result of simple redistribution of any previously hyper-concentrated community of foreigners. Likewise, the increases appear to be beyond the scale of what could be caused purely through foreign nationals giving birth in Japan, suggesting that increased immigration is indeed a major factor in Japan’s expanding foreign resident population.

content:
Plus, an exclusive bag of snacks to sprinkle on ramen, inspired by the iconic instant noodles.

Japanese convenience stores are always coming up with exciting new ways to make hot food more interesting, and 7-Eleven is doing that right now with a brand new fried chicken inspired by the flavour of a beloved mini cup of tonkotsu ramen.

Called “Okashina Chicken (Butamen Tonkotsu Flavour)” this new product has been created in collaboration with Oyatsu Company’s long-running Butamen mini cup ramen brand.

▼ Butamen (ブタメン) literally translates as “Pig Noodle“.

Butamen is a long-selling small cup ramen that first appeared in Japan in 1993. Its tonkotsu flavour, based on the rich pork-bone broth associated with Japanese ramen, proved to be particularly popular, turning Butamen into one of Oyatsu Company’s best-known products.

▼ Butamen comes in many flavours, but tonkotsu is the most popular.

Now, that nostalgic ramen flavour has been turned into a hot snack, with 7-Eleven’s new Okashina Chicken (Butamen Tonkotsu Flavour).

▼ The Okashina Chicken is priced at 198.72 yen (US$1.25) and comes in cute Butamen paper packaging.

“Okashina” translates as “Strange”, and that’s an apt description for this piece of fried chicken as it looks more like a fried doughnut. The unusual doughnut-like ring shape, complete with a hole in the middle, makes it stand out from other products in the hot food display at the counter.

▼ This promo image highlights the candy look of the chicken with a blurb at the top that reads: “Is this a sweet? No, it’s fried chicken!”

Made with chicken breast, the snack has been designed to balance the savoury Butamen-inspired tonkotsu flavour with a crispy coating. Biting into the crunchy fried exterior is said to deliver the familiar rich and savoury flavour of Butamen.

The playful look of the product is all part of the appeal, with 7-Eleven describing it as the sort of food that’s likely to catch people’s attention and inspire photos for social media.

For many locals, this is an unprecedented new way to enjoy the ramen they’ve grown up eating, and 7-Eleven is amping up excitement for the new release with another surprising Butamen product.

▼ Butamen Roast Pork-Style Snack (Pork & Garlic Flavour)

Priced at 140 yen, this limited-edition snack is inspired by the toppings you might add to a bowl of ramen, with a light, crispy texture and a rich pork-and-garlic flavour. It’s designed to be eaten on its own, but Oyatsu Company also recommends crumbling it over a cup of Butamen to give the ramen a roast-pork-style topping. The snack starts out crispy before gradually melting in the mouth, adding another texture to the experience.

▼ Enjoy the ブタメンパラダイス (Butamen Paradise)

Both products will be available at participating 7-Eleven stores nationwide, with the snack going on sale from 10 August and the fried chicken on 11 August.
